lesson.title: Wohnen II: der Teppich, der Schrank, der Spiegel, der Vorhang, der Balkon
lesson.subtitle: a carpet that began in Greek, a wardrobe related to shrink, and a curtain that is a literal hang-before

hook.title: Furniture with Passports
hook.content: der Teppich is the well-travelled one: German took it from Latin tapetium, which took it from Greek tápēs, 'heavy cloth' — and English tapestry descends from the same Greek carpet-word, by way of French tapisserie. der Schrank never left the Germanic house: it shares its ancient root with English shrink — a Schrank was originally the enclosing, bending-in thing, the cabinet that squeezes your clothes into place. der Vorhang is transparent German: vor + hängen, a literal hang-before, built the way English once built compounds before it borrowed 'curtain' from French. der Balkon is a boomerang: a Germanic word for beam, *balko, walked south, became Italian balcone and French balcon, and returned to German as a balcony — while English kept the original beam as balk. der Spiegel keeps its history to itself: from Latin speculum, but with no clean English twin in everyday words, so we leave it honest and unstressed.

footnotes.title: Der Schrank's Family Reunion
footnotes.content: The root behind Schrank and shrink is the Germanic *skrenkw-, 'to bend, to draw in'. English made it a verb (shrink), German made it a noun (der Schrank) — the wardrobe as the thing that 'draws in' what you hang inside it.

pattern.title: Placing the Furniture
pattern.content: 1. Above and below: Der Vorhang ist oben, der Teppich ist unten — position words without articles, the room mapped in two words. 2. At the back: Der Schrank steht hinten — stehen is the furniture verb, and hinten reaches back to Richtung II. 3. Under: Der Teppich ist unter dem Sofa — unter + dem for what lies beneath. 4. Along: Wir gehen den Flur entlang — entlang trails behind its noun phrase when the motion runs the length of it, and the Flur from Wohnen I is the hallway it walks. 5. One loan in the bank: Der Computer ist neu — Wohnen II has room for the machines too.
pattern.linguist_note: English balk survives mostly in the fixed phrase 'balk at' and in baseball's 'balk', but its older sense is a beam or ridge of land — the same Germanic *balko that Italian dressed up as balcone. The beam became a balcony: architecture as etymology.

exercises.prompt: The room, furnished — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The curtain is up top, the rug is down below
matching_pairs.german: Der Vorhang ist oben, der Teppich ist unten

matching_pairs.english: The wardrobe stands at the back
The rug is under the sofa
matching_pairs.german: Der Teppich ist unter dem Sofa

matching_pairs.english: The mirror is on the wall
matching_pairs.german: Der Spiegel ist an der Wand

exercises.target_answer: Der Vorhang ist oben, der Teppich ist unten, Der Schrank steht hinten, Der Teppich ist unter dem Sofa, Der Computer ist neu, Der Spiegel ist an der Wand, Der Balkon ist groß
exercises.meaning: a curtain above and a rug below, a wardrobe at the back, a rug under the sofa, a new computer, a mirror on the wall, a big balcony
exercises.explanation: Five fittings and their places. oben/unten/hinten need no article — they are directions, not nouns — while unter dem Sofa takes the dative because the rug merely lies there.

exercises.prompt: One Germanic word went south, became Italian balcone, and came back dressed as a balcony. Which word here is that boomerang?
exercises.meaning: der Balkon and English balk share the Germanic beam-word *balko
exercises.explanation: *balko meant 'beam'. Italian balcone borrowed it, French passed it on, and German took der Balkon back from the south — while English balk quietly kept the original beam. der Teppich and tapestry share Greek tápēs instead, and der Schrank's cousin shrink never left the verb shelf.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the walk through the flat: 'We walk along the hallway'
exercises.explanation: entlang is the straggler: when the motion runs the length of something, it trails AFTER the noun phrase — den Flur entlang, not entlang den Flur. hinten sits in the bank as the decoy: a direction word, not this postposition.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The curtain is up top and the rug is down below'
exercises.target_answer: Der Vorhang ist oben und der Teppich ist unten
exercises.meaning: The curtain is up top and the rug is down below
exercises.explanation: The room in one sentence: oben and unten divide it vertically, und joins the halves, and every noun keeps der — der Vorhang, der Teppich — because furniture gender in German is fixed at the factory.

exercises.idea: you are showing a friend the living room: the computer is new and the wardrobe is old
cues: der Schrank — the wardrobe, cousin of English shrink
exercises.target_answer: Der Computer ist neu und der Schrank ist alt
exercises.meaning: The computer is new and the wardrobe is old
exercises.explanation: Two loans from different centuries in one sentence: der Computer borrowed in our lifetime, der Schrank pure Germanic — and the alt in the bank reminds you which end of the contrast the wardrobe sits at.

diagnosis.slip: the two clauses lost their second der
diagnosis.cue: und starts a fresh clause, so der Schrank needs its article again — German does not share articles across und the way English shares 'the'.

summary.outcome: Furnish a room in German: place things oben, unten, hinten and unter dem Sofa, walk den Flur entlang, and trace four words back to Greek, Germanic beams and a hang-before.

use_example.german: Der Vorhang ist oben, der Teppich ist unten — der Computer ist neu.
use_example.english: The curtain is up top, the rug is down below — the computer is new.

summary.takeaway: Teppich and tapestry share Greek tápēs, Schrank and shrink share *skrenkw-, Vorhang is vor + hängen, Balkon is the beam-word balk returning from Italy — and der Spiegel keeps its own counsel.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the table is laid — die Gabel, das Messer, die Flasche, der Becher, die Kanne — and a knife that is a 1,500-year-old compound.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Wohnen II: der Teppich, der Schrank, der Spiegel, der Vorhang, der Balkon (The curtain is up top and the rug is down below):
twist.target_answer: Der Vorhang ist oben und der Teppich ist unten
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Der Vorhang ist oben und der Teppich ist unten" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Wohnen II: der Teppich, der Schrank, der Spiegel, der Vorhang, der Balkon without relying on short-term echo.

teppich.context_phrase: Der Teppich liegt unter dem Tisch.
teppich.context_translation: The rug is under the table.
teppich.etymology_derivation: Via Medieval Latin tapicus, from Latin tapes; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

schrank.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *skrankaz 'grid, barrier'; no English cognate — memorize this one (see der Kühlschrank). [wiktionary]

spiegel.context_phrase: Der Spiegel hängt an der Wand.
spiegel.context_translation: The mirror hangs on the wall.
spiegel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *spēgl, an early adoption of Latin speculum; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

vorhang.etymology_derivation: vor (in front) + hängen (hang) — 'the front-hang'; no English cognate. [wiktionary]

balkon.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French balcon, Italian balcone — a Romance loan; no Germanic root. [wiktionary]

oben.context_phrase: Das Buch ist oben auf dem Tisch.
oben.context_translation: The book is up on the table.
oben.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ubanē, kin to über (over); no direct English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

unten.etymology_derivation: Old High German undenân, kin to unter (under); no direct English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

hinten.context_translation: The toilet is at the back on the left.
hinten.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hindanē — the same hind root as English behind and hind; German shifted d to t (the entry points to hinter for the consonantism). [wiktionary]

sofa.context_translation: The sofa is in the living room.
sofa.etymology_derivation: From French sofa, ultimately Arabic ṣuffa — the same loan route as English sofa. [wiktionary]

computer.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English computer - a straight English loan. [wiktionary]

entlang.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Middle Low German entlanc, essentially in lang — the lang element is the twin of English long, so it works just like along. [wiktionary]

flur.context_translation: The shoes are standing in the hallway.
flur.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic floraz; English floor is a direct cognate that kept the old sense, while German Flur narrowed to mean hallway. [wiktionary]

fenster.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *fenestr, an early borrowing of Latin fenestra — a Latin loan both languages share. [wiktionary]

zimmer.context_phrase: Mein Zimmer ist groß und hell.
zimmer.context_translation: My room is big and bright.
zimmer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *timrą — cognate with English timber: English keeps t, German shifted it to z. [wiktionary]

wohnung.context_phrase: Meine Wohnung ist im dritten Stock.
wohnung.context_translation: My apartment is on the third floor.
wohnung.etymology_derivation: Wohnen (to dwell) plus -ung; the page documents the archaic English cognate woning (dwelling-place) from the same dwelling-word. [wiktionary]

etage.context_phrase: Wir wohnen in der dritten Etage.
etage.context_translation: We live on the third floor.
etage.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French étage; English stage is a doublet from the same Old French word estage. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
